question: How many pairs of ribs make up the normal human chest cage?
explanation: Humans typically have twelve pairs of ribs that attach at the back to the spinal column to protect the chest organs. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main job of the costal cartilages in the chest wall?

options.A: Producing red blood cells for the circulatory system
options.B: Preventing the heart from shifting into the right lung
options.C: Anchoring the abdominal muscles to the pelvic girdle
options.D: Providing elasticity to the chest wall during breathing

explanation: Costal cartilages connect the ribs to the breastbone while giving the chest the flexibility to expand and relax as we breathe. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h1)

question: Which rib attaches right next to the sternal angle?
explanation: The sternal angle sits level with the second costal cartilage, which makes it an easy landmark to find when counting ribs during an exam. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h2)

question: What are the three main parts of the adult human breastbone or sternum?
explanation: The sternum is divided from top to bottom into the upper manubrium, the central body, and the lower xiphoid process. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which rib pairs are called floating ribs because they do not attach in the front?
explanation: The eleventh and twelfth ribs are short and do not connect to the sternum or other cartilage, which is why they are called floating ribs. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why are the eighth through tenth ribs called false ribs?

options.A: They remain completely absent in some individuals
options.B: They do not articulate with the thoracic vertebrae
options.C: They are made entirely of bone without cartilage
options.D: They do not attach directly to the sternum

explanation: False ribs attach to the cartilage of the rib just above them instead of connecting straight to the breastbone. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h3)

question: What special feature do thoracic vertebrae have that other back bones generally lack?
explanation: Thoracic vertebrae have specific smooth spots on their bodies and sides designed to connect with the ribs. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which specific structures form the joint at the back of the thorax called the costotransverse joint?

options.A: The rib head and the intervertebral disc
options.B: The sternal angle and the costal cartilage
options.C: The xiphoid process and the seventh rib
options.D: The rib tubercle and the vertebral transverse process

explanation: The costotransverse joint connects the bony bump on the rib to the side projection of the corresponding spine bone. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h4)

question: In what order are the vein, artery, and nerve arranged in the groove along the bottom of a rib from top to bottom?
explanation: The blood vessels and nerve running beneath each rib follow the VAN order, placing the intercostal vein at the top, the artery in the middle, and the nerve at the bottom. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h5)

question: When placing a needle into the chest wall between ribs, why must it go near the upper border of the lower rib?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing severe cardiac arrhythmias
options.B: To avoid damaging the neurovascular bundle tucked under the upper rib
options.C: To ensure the needle enters the muscular layer rather than the lung
options.D: To bypass the thickest portion of the costal cartilage safely

explanation: Blood vessels and nerves run right along the bottom edge of the upper rib, so placing a needle just above the lower rib keeps those structures safe. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h5)

question: What term describes the upward and outward movement of the lower ribs that widens the chest sideways?
explanation: The lower ribs move like the handle of a bucket, lifting outward and upward to widen the chest from side to side when breathing in. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which physical change happens to the chest cage during normal breathing in?

options.A: Its overall volume increases to draw air into the lungs
options.B: Its upper ribs depress to push air out of the airways
options.C: Its transverse diameter decreases to compress the heart
options.D: Its lower ribs move downward to flatten the diaphragm

explanation: When breathing muscles contract, the chest expands in multiple directions, increasing its space and pulling air inside. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h6)

question: What defines the serious chest condition known as a flail chest?

options.A: A single hairline fracture of the first rib near the collarbone
options.B: Inflammation of the intercostal muscles following a viral infection
options.C: Total calcification of the costal cartilages preventing expansion
options.D: Multiple ribs fractured in places creating a free-floating segment

explanation: A flail chest happens when several ribs break in multiple places, creating an unstable wall segment that moves opposite to normal breathing. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h7)

question: Which sign would a clinician expect to see in a patient with a painful rib fracture?

options.A: Profound slowing of the resting heart rate below fifty beats per minute
options.B: Reluctance to take deep breaths due to sharp localized chest pain
options.C: Complete inability to speak or swallow fluids without choking
options.D: Sudden swelling of the lower limbs and prominent ankle edema

explanation: Rib fractures hurt intensely when the chest moves, so patients take shallow breaths to minimize pain, which can lead to reduced airflow in the lungs. [learn more](BMP111_U2_T9#BMP111_U2_T9_h7)
